# Reading a unit's magnitude, compiled and run as Go, then run again on the
# interpreter.
#
# testdata/unit_base_field_interpolation.txtar and unit_duration_cast.txtar say
# what the three targets generate; this says the Go they generate builds and
# answers. That is the claim this whole class of bug needs, because every one
# of them was invisible for the same reason: `sngl generate` wrote something to
# disk and exited 0. `("px is " + m.m.Px)` is a string plus a float64 and did
# not compile at all; `int(d)` compiled and was wrong.
#
# The assertions are on the magnitudes rather than on the text, so the test
# fails if the arithmetic is wrong as well as if the file does not build. A
# test agent reads a component's own state and not a field of it, which is why
# the reads are copied into scalars by a mount effect.
#
# `int(d)` is 500 because a duration's declared base is ms, which is what it
# already was on Kotlin and JavaScript. Go carries the value as a
# time.Duration, whose unit is nanoseconds, and handed that straight out of the
# cast, so this read 500000000 on one target and 500 on the other two. The
# representation is unchanged and only the cast divides.
#
# The second run is why `int(t)` is asserted at all. The `none` platform is the
# interpreter rather than generated code, and its ToInt had no case for a unit
# -- so every `int(<unit>)` was 0 there, which is neither answer. Two runners
# over one program is what states that they agree.
#
# `sum` is the case that needs both runners the most. Every other read here is
# off a literal, which is the one shape where one magnitude and a suffix agree
# with the record -- so a member read off a value arithmetic built is what
# separates the two models, and the interpreter was on the wrong one.

sngl test --platform=bubbletea --language=go app.sngl
stdout 'PASS'
! stdout 'FAIL'

sngl test --platform=none app.sngl
stdout 'PASS'
! stdout 'FAIL'

-- app.sngl --
import . "sngl:test"
import ui "sngl:ui"
import "sngl:time"

unit tick {
    tk
}

component main ui.node {
    var m ui.measurement = 3px
    var r ui.measurement = 2rem
    var sum ui.measurement = m + r
    var t tick = 4tk
    var d time.duration = 500ms
    var widePx = 0.0
    var remEm = 0.0
    var remPx = 0.0
    var sumPx = 0.0
    var sumEm = 0.0
    var ticks = 0.0
    var wholeTicks = 0
    var millis = 0
    var later = 0

    effect(@mount {
        widePx = m.px
        remEm = r.em
        remPx = r.px
        sumPx = sum.px
        sumEm = sum.em
        ticks = float(t)
        wholeTicks = int(t)
        millis = int(d)
        later = int(d + 1s)
    })

    ui.text(value="px is {m.px}")
    ui.text(value="tk is {float(t)}")
    ui.text(value="ms is {int(d)}")
}

func testAPerBaseFieldIsANumber(t Test, c main) {
    t.assert(c.widePx == 3.0)
}

// A reduced suffix counts in the base it reduces to, so 2rem is 32em and no px
// at all -- the record every backend builds, with the bases it was not written
// in left at zero.
func testAReducedSuffixCountsInItsBase(t Test, c main) {
    t.assert(c.remEm == 32.0)
    t.assert(c.remPx == 0.0)
}

// Addition is per base and keeps every one of them: 3px + 32em is not 35 of
// anything. Both reads are off a value arithmetic built rather than off a
// literal, which is the one shape a single magnitude and a suffix can hold --
// the interpreter answered 35 for px and 0 for em while both compiled targets
// answered 3 and 32, and only a two-runner assertion says so.
func testAdditionKeepsEveryBase(t Test, c main) {
    t.assert(c.sumPx == 3.0)
    t.assert(c.sumEm == 32.0)
}

func testASingleBaseUnitConverts(t Test, c main) {
    t.assert(c.ticks == 4.0)
    t.assert(c.wholeTicks == 4)
}

func testADurationConvertsToMilliseconds(t Test, c main) {
    t.assert(c.millis == 500)
    t.assert(c.later == 1500)
}

ui.window {
    main
}
-- testrun/bubbletea/go/app.sngl/main/1 --
